inconsequential

in-kon-suh-KWEN-shuhl -- from Latin in- ('not') + consequi ('to follow along with'), from con- ('with') + sequi ('to follow'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Inconsequential is not important or significant.

Next to the historic peace treaty being signed in the next room, the argument over parking spots felt entirely inconsequential.

Example

A company's board spends an entire hour debating the inconsequential wording of an internal memo while the merger that will decide the company's future waits untouched on the day's schedule.

Inconsequential describes exactly that -- something carrying almost no real importance in the bigger picture, no matter how much attention it gets.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

minor: Minor means small in size or seriousness -- a minor injury, a minor delay -- but minor things can still demand attention and leave a mark. Inconsequential goes further: it says the thing makes no real difference to the outcome at all, however much fuss surrounds it.

incidental: Incidental describes something that happens alongside the main event without being part of its purpose -- incidental expenses on a trip, an incidental detail in a report. Inconsequential is a judgment of weight, not position: whatever the thing is, central or side, it changes nothing that matters.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

pivotal: of crucial importance to a situation's outcome

momentous: of great significance, especially historically

Where it sits · how little difference it makes

unimportant → inconsequential → negligible

unimportant vs. inconsequential: Unimportant is a plain, general word -- almost anything minor can be called unimportant -- while inconsequential adds the specific sense that something has no real effect on the outcome that matters.

negligible vs. inconsequential: Negligible is a bit stronger than inconsequential when describing amounts or effects -- a negligible difference is one so tiny it's barely worth measuring, while inconsequential more often describes an issue or event's overall importance.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: not (Latin)

Prefix — con-: with, together (Latin cum)

Root — sequ: to follow (from Latin sequi, 'to follow')

Suffix — -ential: having the quality of (as in essential) (Latin)

Put it together: In- ('not') + con- ('with, together') + sequ ('to follow' — from Latin sequi) + -ential ('having the quality of,' as in essential): a consequence is what 'follows together with' an action, so something inconsequential does not follow as a meaningful consequence of anything — it carries no real weight.

Use the root in a new word: sequel: The author swears she will never write a sequel, no matter what her publisher offers.

Root Check

Word Choice

Inconsequential describes something's lack of importance relative to a bigger picture -- it's a slightly more formal cousin of 'unimportant,' often used when comparing a minor detail to a much larger event or decision. It should not be confused with "paltry," a nearby word in this unit that describes a disappointingly small amount, especially of money, rather than a lack of importance.
